item.title: Analytical Modeling of Thermal Shield-Induced Tilt Noise in Lunar Regolith: Constraints on Future Lunar Seismometers and Gravitational waves Detectors
item.description: arXiv:2611.26658v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Surface features such as thermal shields, insulating blankets, and exposed rocks modify the absorption of solar radiation in the lunar regolith, producing lateral temperature gradients missed by one-dimensional thermal models. These gradients cause thermoelastic deformation that tilts surface-deployed seismic instruments, adding long-period noise. We develop an analytical framework, based on Hankel transforms in a semi-infinite regolith, that treats these features as perturbations to a laterally uniform diurnal thermal state; linearity allows multiple features to be superposed. The framework is applied to the Apollo 14 Passive Seismic Experiment, including the seismometer thermal shield and surrounding instruments. The Apollo shield is a multilayer insulation (MLI) blanket that passes a fraction of the solar-flux fluctuation to the ground. Near local noon the shadow of the instrument body shifts by 2-5 cm across this dimly lit ground. This asymmetry dominates the tilt; its median amplitude spectral density reaches 7-8 x 10^(-11) rad/sqrt(Hz) in the 1-5 mHz band, about three orders of magnitude above that of an opaque shield. Enlarging an opaque shield lowers the tilt, but the body-shadow tilt of an MLI shield does not decrease with shield radius. Thermal heterogeneity can thus generate a tilt bias, present even during seismically quiet intervals, that should be included in the noise budget of future lunar horizontal seismometers and inertial GW accelerometers, and the optical transmission of the shield and the instrument's own shadow can matter more than shield size. The analytical framework provides a computationally efficient way to evaluate thermal-shield geometry, albedo contrast, and instrument placement for future lunar seismic and inertial gravitational-wave sensor deployments.

item.title: PLATON 7: An ultra-fast exoplanet atmospheric retrieval code
item.description: arXiv:2611.26680v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: PLATON is an open source Python package for atmospheric retrieval, first released in 2018. We introduce PLATON 7, a complete rewrite of PLATON using Claude Fable 5. The biggest changes are that PLATON now uses JAX for all intensive calculations, and these calculations are now performed in single precision instead of double precision. These two changes speed up the code by a factor of ~60 with negligible decrease in accuracy, allowing it to compute a 0.8--5.3 um transmission spectrum at R=20k in 0.35 ms on a RTX 5090. We also introduce several new features, including support for two-limb retrievals, patchy clouds, and more opacities (particularly OCS and CS2). PLATON is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ideasrule/platon.

item.title: Generative Bayesian modelling of radio antenna beams An application to the MeerKAT radio telescope
item.description: arXiv:2611.26713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate primary beam models are essential for high-fidelity calibration and imaging in radio astronomy. Traditional approaches either lack the ability to represent realistic antenna patterns (analytical models) or become computationally prohibitive to interpolate for wide-bandwidth observations (electromagnetic simulations, direct holographic measurements). We develop a generative beam model that represents both the spatial structure and the frequency variations in the primary beam while remaining tractable for integration into calibration and imaging pipelines, achieving superior accuracy compared to existing parametric models and reducing data storage compared to data-based models. We adopt a non-parametric Bayesian framework grounded in information field theory, implemented using the NIFTy library. The model represents the beam as a base pattern subject to frequency-dependent geometric transformations (scaling and shifting). Performance is validated through posterior predictive checks (chi^2/dof ~ 1) and compared against traditional models (Gaussian, Airy disc, JimBeam, Eidos, electromagnetic simulation). We apply the method to holographic data of the array-averaged MeerKAT Stokes I beam in the L band. The model achieves 400:1 data compression while preserving statistical consistency with holographic measurements, and outperforms existing approaches by more than an order of magnitude in mean squared deviation. Zernike decomposition of the base beam, combined with the geometric transformations, enables efficient beam reconstruction at arbitrary spatial resolution. The 150 kB per-antenna footprint enables memory-slim integration into calibration and imaging software at negligible cost, scales favourably to large arrays and wide bandwidths, and can be readily adapted to other radio telescopes.

item.title: Computing the Wave: Bridging Gravitational Wave and High-Energy-Physics software (with modular ROOT extensions)
item.description: arXiv:2611.27026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-Energy Physics (HEP) and Gravitational Wave (GW) astronomy pursue different scientific goals, yet they face strikingly similar computing challenges and can enrich one another through shared software. Building on the prototype presented at ACAT 2024, we report on the consolidation of that work into a single, modular extension of the CERN ROOT data-analysis framework, freely distributed under RIOPlus. The library is now organised as a set of optional, dynamically loadable extensions covering configuration and file-format parsing (including the Gravitational Wave Frame (GWF) format and HDF5), remote and federated data access (OSDF/Pelican, S3, Kafka) with token-based credentials, an enhanced dynamic-display manager, an advanced signal-processing layer built on the KFR library, and a complex-capable tensor layer backed by LibTorch with ONNX interoperability. We summarise the design of each extension, outline the intended application to transient-noise (glitch) detection and classification, and update the FFT performance benchmark comparing KFR with FFTW. We close with the end-to-end ROOT-centred workflow these extensions enable, its current status, and an outlook toward column-wise RNTuple storage.

item.title: Accurately Measuring Variability Properties from Noisy Light Curves
item.description: arXiv:2611.27236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern time-domain surveys probe optical variability near photometric error, challenging weak-signal recovery. The structure function (SF) is widely used for characterizing variability of active galactic nuclei (AGNs), but its statistical recovery limits are unclear. Using simulated light curves with realistic errors, we compare three SF estimators from the literature: two non-parametric (pairwise noise subtraction and Bayesian) and one parametric. All recover intrinsic SF when variability dominates, but diverge in the weak regime. The pairwise noise-subtraction estimator approaches an artificial floor when negative variance estimates are discarded, with the floor set by photometric precision and sampling rather than intrinsic variability. The parametric method suffers degeneracy, while the Bayesian estimator yields nearly unbiased SF estimates given well-calibrated photometric errors and adequate sampling. We also derive an idealized detection threshold linking intrinsic variability, photometric precision, and pair counts, providing a reference for assessing the detectability of weak signals. Our results establish statistical limits for SF measurements in the weak-variability regime and offer a framework for accurately measuring low-amplitude variability in AGNs (e.g., extremely stable quasars) and in new populations such as little red dots discovered by JWST.

item.title: PHOTO-CAT - Photometric Contamination Analyzer Tool: A High-Performance Framework for Photometric Contamination Assessment
item.description: arXiv:2611.27677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-precision photometric missions are sensitive to flux contamination from neighboring stars, which can bias light curves, dilute transit depths, and compromise photometric precision. We present PHOTO-CAT, a catalog-driven, mission-agnostic tool for quantifying stellar flux contamination in photometric observations. The tool builds a three-dimensional Euclidean representation of the sky from a user-provided astrometric catalog, indexes it with a memory-optimized KDTree for rapid neighbor searches, and computes per-target contamination metrics from angular separation, relative fluxes, and configurable aperture models (top-hat or circular Gaussian PSF), optionally converted into an arbitrary instrumental bandpass via empirical photometric relations or stellar spectral models. A streaming, CSR-style storage format with compact internal identifiers enables scalable processing of catalogs with tens to hundreds of millions of sources with minimal memory overhead. Outputs include per-target contaminating flux, contamination ratios, target purity, number of neighboring sources, and their angular separations, supporting target screening and field-selection decisions ahead of observations. We demonstrate the software performance on all-sky Gaia samples (G <= 12, with neighbors down to G = 17; over three million targets), providing global contamination statistics and spatial characterization of crowded regions, and apply it to the Ariel Mission Candidate Sample to show how wavelength-dependent contamination estimates support target selection and observing-geometry optimization. Although developed for the Mauve satellite, PHOTO-CAT is mission-agnostic and readily applicable to TESS, PLATO, Ariel, and other surveys.

item.title: The Time Domain Telescope: A Global Spectroscopic Array
item.description: arXiv:2611.27758v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Time Domain Telescope (TDT) is an initiative in the context of the ESO Expanding Horizons program. The TDT project aims for a global telescope array for spectroscopic time-resolved and time-critical observations in the optical-near-infrared, with a core at the European Southern Observatory and partners around the world. The TDT core consists of 100 unit telescopes of 2-meter diameter each that are fully Adaptive Optics-assisted in the blue, to deliver an enclosed energy of >=80% within 0.12" at 400nm. The unit telescopes are coupled to a set of spectrographs covering spectral resolutions R=10^3 - 10^5 over the wavelength range 0.35 - 1.8 micrometer. The combination of extreme adaptive optics with near-read-noise-free detectors will allow the TDT to reach unprecedented depths and/or high cadence. When all 100 units target a single object a depth of 25 mag can be reached in 30 minutes at a signal-to-noise ratio of 10 per spectral resolution element at a spectral resolution of R=5000. With this the TDT will spectroscopically match the imaging depth of the Vera Rubin Observatory and the Euclid and Roman spacecrafts, the expected brightness of electromagnetic counterparts discovered by the LISA space mission, as well as by the next-generation gravitational wave detectors. The science of the TDT covers a large part of astronomy, and ranges from the outer Solar System, to stellar and binary systems to extragalactic transients and the growth of supermassive black holes, all the way back to the expansion history of the Universe. The TDT is transformational, unique and highly complementary to the current and near-future ESO facilities, in particular by providing the possibility for time-resolved spectroscopic observations well below the brightness of the optical night sky.

item.title: TDI-$\infty$ and beyond
item.description: arXiv:2611.27761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-delay interferometry (TDI) cancels the laser frequency noise that dominates the measurements of the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA), and relies on interpolating the laser noise to fractional delays. In TDI-$\infty$, which finds the laser noise free combinations from a linear model of the measurements, the interpolation sets the design matrix, and any interpolation error leaves uncanceled laser noise which is not accounted for. We introduce Gaussian process (GP) interpolation into TDI-$\infty$, which models the laser noise from its spectrum and propagates its interpolation error into the likelihood as a covariance. We test it on a realistic data model in which the measurements pass through the on-board anti-alias filter and are downsampled to the 4 Hz telemetry rate, either applying the filter after the delays, as on the spacecraft, or building the filter into the GP kernel. We compare it with Lagrange and cosine-sum interpolation, and also keep the column space of the design matrix, which the standard null space likelihood discards. In lisainstrument simulations all three interpolators cancel the laser noise for a 1 Hz filter band edge, but only the GP does so up to the 2 Hz Nyquist frequency, a range the Lagrange and cosine-sum interpolators were not designed for. In parameter estimation on 200 simulated galactic binaries, the GP with the filter in its kernel gives the smallest calibrated posteriors. The differences are small for a single long data segment and grow when the data are split into short chunks or contain gaps, where the column space also recovers some information, by an amount that depends on the threshold that defines the null space.

item.title: Physics-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement of Amortized Bayesian Inference Across Physics
item.description: arXiv:2611.27006v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Across physics, from the orbits of imaged exoplanets and the matter inside neutron stars to thin films at synchrotrons and cortical neurons, conservation laws, interference, and compensating currents compress the posteriors of precise data into tiny, curved regions where Markov chains need minutes to days. We introduce PhyRSI (physics-guided recursive self-improvement), in which an AI agent coupled to the simulator writes and revises an amortized Bayesian inference algorithm for each field, scored by the importance weights of the exact likelihood because the true posterior is unknown. It evolves coordinates, symmetries, and factorizations matched to the physics: orbital elements at the best-measured epoch, Fresnel-normalized reflectivity with a chart for each of its multiple solutions, coordinates along which Na+ and K+ currents compensate, a shared neutron-star equation of state that factorizes a 32-dimensional joint analysis, and the time-rescaling symmetry of predator-prey dynamics. In six fields, networks trained once on simulations return 36 posteriors of real observations in seconds, reweighted by the likelihood and agreeing with converged Markov chains about as closely as two independent chains agree with each other. Such posteriors could steer synchrotron film growth and patch-clamp recordings as they run, follow X-ray transients while they are bright, update the dense-matter equation of state as neutron stars are added, and compare physical models across catalogs. Inference can thus be evolved and checked by the physics itself rather than designed by hand for each problem.

item.title: Coronagraphic time-delay interferometry: fundamental steps towards concrete applications
item.description: arXiv:2611.27651v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) is a future space-based gravitational wave (GW) observatory. Central to LISA data analysis is time-delay interferometry (TDI), which reduces otherwise overwhelming laser frequency noise. In previous work, we explored coronagraphic TDI, a sky-dependent null-stream channel which cancels the GW signal of a point-like source when pointed at its sky position. Because this property relies only on the geometric response of LISA, coronagraphic TDI is a candidate for model-agnostic sky localization. Here, we address three challenges which arise when analyzing realistic LISA data: (i) spacecraft motion; (ii) signal superposition; (iii) instrumental noise. We derive a second-generation coronagraphic TDI variable and its analytic noise model, and show that it reduces laser frequency noise in the presence of spacecraft motion while still recovering the position of the source. Using pairs of Galactic binaries (GBs), we find that sources can be localized independently provided they do not overlap in frequency, even when they share the same sky position, whereas sources overlapping in frequency can only be localized if one dominates by a factor of ~100 in amplitude. This is confirmed by the analysis of a simulation containing a massive black hole binary and 49 verification GBs. Finally, we introduce a statistical test based on the analytic noise model, which provides well-calibrated confidence regions for the sky position of the source. Applying it to GBs in the presence of instrumental noise, we find that the geometric response alone only weakly constrains the sky position: even at signal-to-noise ratios of order 10^4, 90% confidence regions span ~10^3 deg^2. These are fundamental steps towards applications of coronagraphic TDI to LISA data, such as sky localization and glitch discrimination, which we discuss.
item.dc:creator: Raissa Costa Barroso, Yves Lemi\`ere, Ian Harry

item.title: Precise Interstellar Extinction Estimates for Nearly Ten Million Stars Based on Multiple Spectroscopic Surveys
item.description: arXiv:2611.27773v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate interstellar extinction estimates are vital for revealing the intrinsic physical properties of stars and the dynamic structure of the Milky Way. Based on multiple optical and near-infrared spectroscopic surveys, including LAMOST, APOGEE, GALAH, GaiaESO, SEGUE, and DESI, we use MLPs and polynomial regressions to calibrate giants and dwarfs separately onto the APOGEE parameter scale, constructing a combined spectroscopic catalog of nearly ten million stars with calibrated stellar atmospheric parameters. This catalog not only provides a robust dataset for our extinction measurements, but also serves as a reference sample for estimating stellar parameters from photometric surveys. Both cross-survey comparisons and external comparisons with high-resolution spectroscopic benchmarks show good agreement in the calibrated parameters. By applying the star-pair method to this extensive sample, we obtain precise extinction estimates. Incorporating distance information, we characterize the spatial distribution of extinction covering over 33,000 square degrees of the sky. Comparisons with existing literature demonstrate that our extinction estimates achieve an exceptional precision of 0.019-0.022 mag. The value-added catalog and open-source Python pipeline for line-of-sight extinction released in this work will provide robust support for future Galactic structure studies and photometric calibrations.
item.dc:creator: Bao-Kun Sun, Qiu-Ling Yan, Qing-Guo, Jin-Hua Yang, Yan-Hui Chen, Zheng-Yu, Bai-Song Zhang

item.title: Diffusing the assumptions: towards realistic LISA stochastic component separation with physics-aware simulation-based inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.27848v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Simultaneous global-fit inference of the numerous sources observed by the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) depends on accurate modeling of its stochastic components: instrumental noise, the Galactic foreground, and astrophysical or stochastic gravitational wave backgrounds (SGWB). Realistic features such as non-Gaussian transients and data gaps challenge traditional likelihood-based pipelines, creating an opportunity for simulation-based inference (SBI) to augment traditional analyses. Here, we present an SBI framework for LISA stochastic component separation built on the Simformer, a transformer trained with diffusion or flow matching that ingests the full time-delay interferometry cross-spectral matrix via a physics-aware embedding. We progressively relax standard simplifying assumptions on simulated 11.6-day datasets containing a loud foreground and a faint power-law SGWB. With unequal arms and per-link noise freedom, the networks match 17-dimensional MCMC posteriors after importance reweighting; full cross-spectra constrain each link's optical metrology noise amplitude to $1\%$. When marginalizing over glitches or massive black hole binary transients, estimation errors remain flat up to transient signal-to-noise ratios of several hundred, whereas ignoring them severely biases likelihood fits. Under time-varying spline noise levels, realistic glitch rates, and gaps up to one day long, posterior coverage remains nominal or conservative across $\sim 10^4$ simulations. We test coverage in the local neighborhood of a given observation by introducing a novel importance-weighted localized simulation-based calibration test. We find flow matching slightly better calibrated than diffusion in simpler regimes and observe modest gains from physics-aware template inputs. Finally, we outline how these networks can initialize the noise and stochastic blocks of a LISA global fit.

item.title: Successful irradiation campaign on PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics (PRIMA)/PRIMAger Kinetic Inductance Detectors with the Detector irRAdiation Cryogenic faciLity for Astrophysics (DRACuLA)
item.description: arXiv:2604.23216v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: DRACuLA (Detector irRAdiation Cryogenic faciLity for Astrophysics) is a mobile dilution refrigerator platform developed at the Institut d'Astrophysique Spatiale (IAS) to expose sub-Kelvin detectors to particle beams at their nominal operating temperature, in the range 50 - 300 mK. We report on its design, beam-line integration at the Particle Therapy Research Center (PARTREC) in Groningen, and the operational performance achieved during the September 2025 irradiation campaign on Kinetic Inductance Detector (KID) arrays developed by SRON for the PRIMA mission. The detector samples were maintained at 120 mK throughout a 12-hour proton irradiation run at 184 MeV. The scientific results of this campaign are reported in a companion paper.

item.title: Inpainting to search for premerger massive black hole binaries in realistic LISA datasets
item.description: arXiv:2605.13738v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A key science target of the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) is to carry out multi-messenger observations of massive black hole binaries, observing the merger simultaneously in gravitational waves and with electromagnetic observatories. Identifying that a merger is happening and providing an updating estimate of the sky location in the hours, days and weeks before the merger is critical to enable electromagnetic observations of the merger event. In this work we demonstrate and compare two methods for premerger identification of massive black hole binaries; a zero-latency filter approach and, for the first time, an approach using an ``inpainting'' technique. We apply these methods to the LISA Data Challenge dataset 2a--Sangria-HM--and demonstrate the successful recovery of the 14 signals in the dataset that we expected to be identifiable at least half a day before merger. We show that the inpainting method can identify premerger signals even when gaps are present in the data, demonstrating the recovery of a signal even when 3 day-long data gaps are added to the 14 days preceding merger. Finally, we explore the challenge of overlapping signals, using a region of overlapping signals in the Sangria-HM dataset, all of which merge within a 10-day window, and show how removing signals that have been confidently identified from the data allows us to identify quieter signals in the same period.
item.dc:creator: Gareth Cabourn Davies, Ian Harry

item.title: Extinction by non-spherical particles with the Nanoparticle Transition Matrix Code: perspectives for interstellar medium and exoplanetary atmospheres
item.description: arXiv:2610.17081v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Transition Matrix formalism (T-matrix) offers an optimal solution to the problem of radiation scattering and absorption by particles characterized by a high degree of chemical and structural complexity. However, its application to particle models composed by large numbers of constituents has been classically limited by the substantial computational burden of the method. As a consequence, the investigation of light scattering and absorption processes, in cases where particle asymmetry and non-homogeneity play an important role, typically need to rely on simplifying assumptions which affect the correct interpretation of transmission spectra and extinction curves. This problem has a huge impact on many fields of scientific application. In particular, it has a critical role in astrophysics, because the ability to model highly non homogeneous particles is a fundamental requirement to understand the role of extinction in different phases of the interstellar medium (ISM), as well as to probe the physics of light transmission in planetary atmospheres within the Solar System and beyond. In this work we describe the application of a new implementation of the T-matrix formalism, based on the framework originally developed by Borghese, Denti & Saija and named Nano-particle Transition Matrix code, which leverages the power of modern hardware architectures to reduce the computational costs related to the solution of relevant particle models for the investigation of dust in the ISM and of hot-Jupyter class planets atmospheric aerosols. This new implementation of the T-matrix formalism can handle calculations of increasing complexity with a direct impact in the interpretation of the transmission spectra of transiting exoplanets produced by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and of those expected from the Atmospheric Remote-sensing Infrared Exoplanet Large survey (ARIEL).

item.title: Multi-Method Machine Learning Classification of Astronomical Sources with Rubin Data Previews: a Spectroscopy-Free Approach with DP1 and DP2
item.description: arXiv:2610.20746v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a multi-method machine-learning study for the binary photometric classification of point-like and extended sources in the Rubin Observatory Data Preview 1 (DP1) and Data Preview 2 (DP2). The workflow runs on the Rubin Science Platform using DP1 and DP2 ugrizy photometry, the DP1 ancillary photometric-redshift catalog, and the Monster astrometric and photometric reference catalog, without relying on external spectroscopy. Six methods (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, k-Nearest Neighbors, an Artificial Neural Network, and a soft Voting ensemble) are benchmarked in the deepest DP1 field, the Extended Chandra Deep Field South. These methods reach 10-fold cross-validation macro-F1 scores of 0.95-0.97 on the balanced training subset and test macro-F1 scores of 0.87-0.92 on the imbalanced held-out set, with RF and the SV ensemble tied at the top (0.918); the differences among the leading methods are within the statistical uncertainty. Permutation importance identifies FWHM as the dominant feature, and the six methods agree on 79.5% of the full catalog. The same pipeline is then applied without retuning the settings to the two other DP1 fields with full ugrizy coverage and photometric-redshift support, Euclid Deep Field South and the Low Galactic Latitude Field. Together, the three fields span a factor of approximately 7 in E(B-V) and approximately 10 in stellar density, yet headline macro-F1 remains above 0.87 in every field. We then apply the same pipeline to four DP2 fields (ECDFS, COSMOS, EDFS, and ELAIS-S1). Using colors and morphology, the best method reaches a test macro-F1 of 0.83 to 0.88 across these fields, and the six methods agree on 77 to 86% of each catalog. Adding the per-band photometric uncertainties as features raises the best macro-F1 to about 0.95 in ECDFS DP1 and 0.97 in ECDFS DP2 (and to approximately 0.97-0.98 in the other fields).

item.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). An overview of the Science Ground Segment architecture and operations
item.description: arXiv:2611.16480v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Euclid mission is designed to address fundamental questions on the nature of dark energy and dark matter by mapping the extragalactic sky with a wide-area survey complemented by targeted deep observations. The required scientific performance places stringent demands on the Euclid Science Ground Segment (SGS), which transforms raw telemetry into calibrated, validated, and scientifically exploitable products. The SGS is a distributed system comprising the Euclid Science Operations Centre, the Science Data Centres, Instrument Operation Teams, and supporting Organisation Units, within a common architectural and procedural framework. This paper presents the SGS as implemented for Data Release 1 (DR1), describing its organisation, architecture, processing functions, and operational model. We outline the main components of the SGS common infrastructure. A key element is the Euclid Archive System (EAS), the central metadata repository based on a common data model. It comprises a Distributed Storage System, providing scalable storage of data files across the Science Data Centres; a Data Processing System used by the pipelines to register and access files and their lineage; and a Science Archive, distributing validated data products. Processing is coordinated by a common orchestration framework based on the Infrastructure Abstraction Layer, providing workflow management and resource abstraction of distributed compute clusters. Software development, integration, and deployment are supported by the Common Development Environment. We describe daily operations, calibration, and quality control, followed by the DR1 production campaign, including processing flows, validation strategy, and computational and data volumes. This infrastructure enabled Euclid DR1, involving 35 million jobs across nine Science Data Centres and 6.7 million core-hours, demonstrating robustness and scalability of the SGS.

item.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1): NISP-P point-spread function modelling pipelines
item.description: arXiv:2611.16494v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The images collected in photometric mode by the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) instrument of the Euclid satellite are used to model the point-spread function (PSF) of a selection of sources detected in single and combined frames. We used Q1 and DR1 data to improve the development of the PSF module of the near-infrared processing function (NIR PF) and to refine the models currently provided. We explored a few methods normally used to evaluate the quality of the derived models and discuss possible variations related to the position of the sources in the focal plane and to the wavelength and time of the observations. The procedure of fitting the PSF profile, compared to other methods used for flux estimation, such as aperture photometry, indicates that updated models are better than those provided by Q1 images. The current results are in agreement with several key requirements defined for the mission, but there is still room for further improvements, which we plan to investigate and implement in future releases.

item.title: The 2MIG isolated AGNs. 3. Optical--IR variability and dust reverberation in the NLSy1 galaxies Mrk~42 and Mrk~493
item.description: arXiv:2605.06517v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate optical and mid-infrared variability in two isolated narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies, Mrk 42 and Mrk 493, using ZTF and WISE/NEOWISE light curves supplemented by ATLAS, SDSS, Swift, and IAC80 data. We examine colour-magnitude and flux-flux relations and measure optical-to-infrared lags with interpolated cross-correlation functions and flux-randomisation/random-subset-selection (FR/RSS), after correcting WISE fluxes for variable accretion-disc emission. For Mrk 42, the observed-frame W1 and W2 lags are 54 (+13/-33) and 62 (+7/-35) d, corresponding to redshift- and wavelength-corrected dust-response radii of 0.045 (+0.011/-0.028) and 0.052 (+0.006/-0.029) pc. For Mrk 493, the lags are 94 (+18/-21) and 111 (+26/-24) d, yielding radii of 0.078 (+0.015/-0.017) and 0.092 (+0.021/-0.020) pc. Both galaxies become optically bluer when brighter, but their W1-W2 colour responses differ: a significant relation is found in Mrk 493, whereas host and circumnuclear dilution may weaken it in Mrk 42. SDSS spectral decomposition provides a host-corrected AGN luminosity for comparison with the broad-line region in Mrk 42. The dust radii are consistent with the low-luminosity extension and scatter of published dust-radius--bolometric-luminosity relations. Mrk 42 also exhibits four broad maxima within a major optical flare, with a characteristic 45-47 d timescale; non-uniform peak intervals and stochastic-model tests favour substructure in a larger accretion-driven event. The results support disc-to-hot-dust reverberation in both galaxies while revealing distinct colour and optical-variability behaviour.

item.title: CARMApy: An Open-Source Python Framework for Simulating Microphysical Clouds in Planetary Atmospheres
item.description: arXiv:2606.30438v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: CARMApy is a new open-source python code that performs bin-scheme microphysical modeling of clouds in exoplanet atmospheres. It models key cloud properties such as particle size distributions and microphysical rates from first principles. The code is a wrapper of ExoCARMA, a well tested Fortran code with an almost half century long heritage. CARMApy includes the microphysical processes of homogeneous and heterogeneous nucleation, condensational growth, evaporation, coagulation, and vertical transport. CARMApy has 10 built-in default condensates and allows the user to specify additional condensates. In this work we describe CARMApy and the data products that it can generate, along with the history of its code heritage. We additionally compile a complete description of the theory and methods used in CARMA. Lastly we benchmark CARMApy and show that its results are consistent with previous versions of CARMA, while executing the code ~1.9 times faster single threaded ~3.8 times faster multithreaded.

item.title: Probabilistic redshift estimation of undetected galaxies from multi-band background light maps
item.description: arXiv:2607.14525v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurate knowledge of the redshift distributions of undetected galaxy populations is essential for extracting the cosmological information encoded in the cosmic optical background. We present the first framework for estimating these distributions directly from multi-band maps of unresolved background light, using conditional normalising flows trained on realistic image simulations. For imaging quality comparable to that expected from the Euclid survey and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), our model achieves sub-per cent accuracy in both the mean and standard deviation of the flux-weighted redshift distributions when the training and target samples are statistically well matched. Furthermore, the network proves highly resilient to incomplete photometric coverage when combined with tailored data imputation strategies. To address the challenge of statistical mismatches between simulations and real observations, we propose incorporating observational quantities into the target variables, providing a built-in diagnostic to assess model reliability and uncertainty from the predictions themselves. We also demonstrate the feasibility of map-based tomographic analyses, showing that the model retains sufficient pixel-level detail to recover redshift distributions for tomographically defined subsamples with near sub-per cent accuracy across all bins.
item.dc:creator: Shun-Sheng Li, Hendrik Hildebrandt, Ludovic Van Waerbeke

item.title: Reference-Filter-Driven Transition Probabilities for IMM-Based Satellite Maneuver Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.11242v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Detecting maneuvers of non-cooperative satellites is essential for space situational awareness. The interacting multiple model (IMM) filter has been applied to detect unannounced maneuvers, but the standard IMM assumes a fixed Markov transition probability matrix (TPM) that must be tuned without knowledge of the maneuver rate of the target. To avoid the tuning, adaptive-TPM approaches update the TPM online from statistics computed inside the IMM. However, the statistics already depend on the TPM through the interaction step, and the dependence forms a feedback loop. The loop itself can raise the maneuver probability in the absence of a maneuver or suppress its rise when a maneuver occurs. In this paper, the TPM is driven by the normalized innovation squared (NIS) of a reference coast filter that is decoupled from the IMM, and the NIS is mapped continuously to the coast-to-maneuver transition probability. The reference-driven IMM (RD-IMM) is evaluated with four space-based optical sensors tracking a geostationary target. In the simulation, the reference filter keeps its sensitivity after small maneuvers, whereas the NIS of the coast sub-filter of the IMM is reduced by the interaction step. RD-IMM detects 1-3 m/s maneuvers, which the fixed-TPM IMM rarely detects, with a false-declaration rate below the false-alarm probability of 0.05 set for the reference filter. In the first hour after the 1-3 m/s maneuvers, RD-IMM also has a lower position error than the compared filters.
